content.title: About
content.content: Baked beans are a dish made from cooked beans, usually navy or brown beans, simmered in a sauce of tomatoes, sugar, spices and often smoked meat. They are commonly served in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as a side or a standalone item.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baked beans first appeared in the United States in the early 1900s as a workers’ meal.
The classic recipe includes brown beans, molasses, mustard, and spices such as paprika and black pepper.
In the United Kingdom, baked beans are a staple of the traditional breakfast.
Vegetarian versions omit meat and achieve a smoky flavor with liquid smoke or smoked paprika.
The high acidity of the sauce allows canned beans to be stored for long periods.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help with oxygen transport and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The combination of beans and tomato sauce leads to a slower rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomatoes and spices supply lycopene and other antioxidants.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional sauces often contain molasses or added sugar, which can be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Canned versions can be very salty; low‑sodium options are recommended for people with hypertension.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve baked beans hot as a side to meat, potatoes, or in burgers. They can be added to salads, used as a taco filling, or simply eaten with a spoon as a quick snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep an unopened can in a cool, dark place for up to 12 months. Once opened, transfer to a sealed container, refrigerate, and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if mold appears or the smell becomes off.

chicken-breast-grilled-with-sauce-skin-n.title: Chicken breast, grilled with sauce, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken breast is a lean source of protein often grilled with a variety of sauces. Grilling retains most nutrients while the lack of skin reduces saturated fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides more protein per 100 g than most other meat cuts.
Grilling creates a distinctive flavor through Maillard reactions.
Sauces can be tomato‑based, yogurt‑based, honey‑glazed, or soy‑based, altering the taste profile.
Chicken is one of the oldest domesticated animals, kept for over 8,000 years.
When properly cooked, the breast stays juicy despite being skin‑less.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of skinless chicken breast contains about 31 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Without skin, the breast has less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, most of which are polyunsaturated.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Approximately 165 kcal per 100 g, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people can be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain high salt; monitor sodium intake if needed.

items.title: Potential carcinogen formation
items.content: Excessive charring can produce heterocyclic amines; avoid burning the meat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the grilled breast hot as a main dish, slice it for salads, add to sandwiches, or incorporate into pasta dishes. Sauces can be served on the side or drizzled over the meat just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 9 months. Thaw in the fridge, and cooked leftovers can be refrigerated for up to 3 days.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and meat

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and meat is a dish made from eggs, dairy, and meat ingredients. Eggs provide high‑quality protein and nutrients, cheese adds calcium and flavor, and meat contributes extra protein and a savory taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
Cheese boosts the calcium and vitamin D content of the dish.
Meat (such as ham or bacon) adds rich flavor and iron.
Traditionally, omelets are cooked over medium heat to keep a soft texture.
The dish is popular worldwide, from American breakfasts to European appetizers.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs and meat together provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium for bone health, while vitamin D aids its absorption.

items.title: Iron and vitamin B12
items.content: Meat supplies iron and vitamin B12, important for blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat promotes long‑lasting fullness.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and meat can be high in saturated fats, so portion control is advised, especially for heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or cheese.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol levels should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Processed meat additions are often salty, increasing sodium intake.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in grated cheese and finely chopped meat. Heat a small amount of oil in a skillet, pour in the mixture, and cook over medium heat, stirring gently until the eggs set but remain tender. Optionally add herbs, spices, or vegetables for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a little oil to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog is a ready‑to‑eat sausage link, usually made from beef, pork, or a blend, placed in a soft bun. The product is popular in street food, fast‑food outlets, and sporting events. The NFS (No‑Frills Snack) version is a simplified recipe with minimal additives, lower salt and preservative levels.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hot dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century and quickly became an icon of American street cuisine.
The term “hot dog” originated from a joke about the original sausage being made from dog meat, which is a myth.
In Japan, “rice hot dogs” are popular, where the bun is replaced by a sheet of nori with rice.
Sales of NFS versions surged in the 2020s due to increased demand for lower‑sodium snacks.
Hot dogs are often served with a variety of toppings: mustard, ketchup, pickles, onions, and cheese.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The sausage link provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, helping to maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Meat in hot dogs supplies heme iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: The NFS version contains less fat than traditional hot dogs, making it more suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Thermally processed meat is quickly digested, providing a rapid energy boost.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Hot dogs can be high in salt; the NFS version is reduced but still requires moderate consumption.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some variants use nitrites for color preservation, which can be harmful in excess.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain meats (e.g., pork) may react to the product.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: One hot dog (≈100 g) contains roughly 250–300 kcal; portion size should fit the overall daily balance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot dogs are usually heated on a grill, skillet, or microwave, then placed in a split bun. Add mustard, ketchup, pickles, onions, cheese, or fresh vegetables to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at +2…+4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container, up to 5 days. Frozen hot dogs store for up to 3 months; fully thaw and reheat before consumption.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-made-with-light-.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Light Creamy Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with a light creamy dressing is a cold dish where cooked pasta is tossed with a smooth yogurt‑ or mayo‑based dressing, vegetables, herbs, and sometimes bits of ham or cheese. It is popular as a light lunch, snack, or picnic food.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pasta salads are especially popular in summer because they can be made ahead and served chilled.
The creamy dressing can be based on yogurt, sour cream, mayonnaise, or a blend, allowing control over calories.
Different countries favor different pasta shapes: Italy often uses penne, the US prefers rotini, and in Russia spaghetti cut into bite‑size pieces is common.
Adding fresh vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers, and bell peppers boosts the vitamin content.
The dish can be easily adapted to vegetarian or gluten‑free diets by using gluten‑free pasta.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides quickly digestible energy, useful for active people and children.

items.title: Fiber boost (when vegetables are added)
items.content: Vegetables increase dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Both the pasta and added ingredients (cheese, ham, legumes) supply plant and/or animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta is a source of thiamine, niacin, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Low fat when using a light dressing
items.content: A yogurt‑based or light mayo dressing keeps the dish lower in calories than traditional creamy sauces.

items.title: Gluten allergy or celiac disease
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives should be used for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Dressings can be salty; people with hypertension should monitor salt levels.

items.title: Calorie density with cheese or mayo
items.content: Rich additives increase energy intake, so portion size matters for weight‑control diets.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Store the salad refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days to prevent spoilage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, either as a main dish or a side to meat or fish. It is easy to eat with a fork or spoon and convenient to pack in a container for work or school.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 3 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: Pink beans (varieties of Phaseolus vulgaris) are cooked beans with a light pink hue that develops during soaking and boiling. They have a soft, mildly sweet flesh, a gentle nutty aroma, and a pleasant texture. They are used in salads, side dishes, soups, and vegetarian meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The pink color appears after soaking and cooking, not in the raw bean.
Beans belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
In some cultures they are called “red” or “pink” beans, although they are not a separate cultivar.
Heat treatment destroys anti‑nutrients such as phytic acid, improving mineral absorption.
Pink beans are popular in Mexican and South American cuisines.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked pink beans provides about 15 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for hemoglobin formation and nerve‑muscle function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Cooked beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phytochemicals such as flavonoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Despite cooking, small amounts of phytic acid can reduce iron and zinc absorption.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause bloating in sensitive people; introduce them gradually into the diet.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Canned beans may contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add pink beans to salads, pastas, chili, soups, and stews. They work well in vegetarian patties or as a side dish for meat. For extra flavor, briefly sauté them with olive oil and your favorite spices before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pink beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portioned bags – they keep well for up to 3 months. Discard any beans with off‑odors or signs of spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna salad with Italian dressing is a ready‑to‑eat dish featuring cooked or canned tuna combined with vegetables, herbs, and a dressing made from olive oil, vinegar, and classic Italian seasonings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the richest sources of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart and brain health.
Italian dressing often includes oregano, basil, and garlic, giving the salad a Mediterranean aroma.
The salad is convenient for on‑the‑go meals: it requires no heating and stays tasty for several hours when refrigerated.
Canned tuna is usually packed in its own juice or oil, which influences the final calorie count of the salad.
In many countries, tuna salads are a traditional dish for summer picnics.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help lower triglyceride levels and support vascular health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Tuna provides all essential amino acids, supporting muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: The salad fits well into low‑carbohydrate diets and helps regulate blood sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from veggies
items.content: Tomatoes, cucumbers, and greens add vitamin C and lycopene, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: People allergic to seafood may experience reactions to tuna.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Mercury exposure
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Acidic dressing
items.content: The vinegar‑based dressing may irritate sensitive stomachs; reduce vinegar if needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a main dish or alongside bread, wraps, or rice. It stores well in an airtight container for lunch or picnics.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad refrigerated at 0–4 °C in a sealed container for up to 3 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
